extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and students seeking an encyclopedic overview of QAnon
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of QAnon covering its core beliefs, recruitment techniques, demographics, notable incidents, media and political amplification, and official responses. Useful as a reference for understanding what QAnon is and how it has manifested in politics and online activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core QAnon beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: The central claim that 'Donald Trump has been secretly fighting a group of child sex traffickers that include prominent Democrats and Hollywood elites' and the related tenet that global elites form a group of Satan-worshipping pedophiles and child sex traffickers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites multiple polls and surveys quantifying belief in these claims (e.g., 14–19% of Americans across years; higher shares among Trump supporters and certain religious groups). These core beliefs are the defining content used to identify QAnon adherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of QAnon adherence (symbols, slogans, behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of specific slogans, symbols and behaviors—e.g., the slogan WWG1WGA ('Where we go one, we go all'), referring to Trump as 'Q+', reposting 'Q drops', wearing Q-related attire, taking the 'digital soldiers' oath, and participating in Q-oriented events and message boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include visible clothing and emblems at the Capitol, public figures and supporters using WWG1WGA, and coordinated online actions (hashtags, reposting Q content). These markers have been used to identify participants in real-world events (e.g., January 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastel QAnon indoctrination techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of techniques (termed 'Pastel QAnon') aimed predominantly at indoctrinating women via social media by co-opting influencer aesthetics and language, using personal anecdotes and gateway issues such as child sex‑trafficking to frame QAnon beliefs as reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets platforms like Instagram, Facebook, Telegram and YouTube; the approach emphasizes subtle aesthetic and narrative tactics instead of overt 'drops' to recruit and radicalize audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: FBI domestic terrorism threat assessment criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The FBI identified QAnon-driven extremists as a domestic terrorism threat, assessing that conspiracy theories are 'very likely' to emerge, spread, and evolve in the modern information marketplace and 'occasionally' drive groups and individuals to criminal or violent acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FBI memo provided a baseline for future intelligence products and placed conspiracy-theory-driven threats alongside other domestic terrorism categories; it cites arrests and incidents tied to QAnon as evidence for the assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional resolution recommended countermeasures
rubrics_metrics.description: A bipartisan House resolution condemning QAnon that urged law enforcement and homeland security agencies to strengthen efforts to prevent violence, threats, harassment, and other criminal activity by extremists motivated by fringe political conspiracy theories, and to investigate foreign support or amplification of QAnon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolution H. Res. 1154 passed 371–18; the page documents both the resolution's language and the political context (including threats to sponsors), showing the kinds of institutional actions Congress recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of radicalization and post-disillusionment recruitment risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Disillusionment after failed prophecies (e.g., Biden's inauguration) can lead hardline QAnon adherents to be recruited by other extremist movements (alt-right, white nationalists, neo‑Nazis), or to migrate to derivative movements (e.g., the Sabmyk Network) that repurpose QAnon beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and analysts warned that the community's fragmentation could result in recruitment by other violent groups; examples include Telegram channels and new leader-prophet narratives that target disillusioned followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of mainstream political and media influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of QAnon's reach and influence include amplification by prominent politicians and media figures (retweets and reposts by Trump, appearances by followers at rallies), coverage and occasional endorsement by media outlets or public personalities, and adoption of Q‑associated language in political messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents Trump's repeated amplification of QAnon-affiliated accounts, appearances of Q-aligned figures at official events, and media coverage levels (e.g., Time listing Q among influential internet phenomena). These phenomena are used as evidence of QAnon's penetration into mainstream discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world incident and violence linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral outcomes tied to QAnon include vandalism, threats, arrests, participation in the January 6 U.S. Capitol attack, and involvement in plots (e.g., the 2022 German coup plot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page provides concrete examples (America's Stonehenge vandalism, arrests for criminal mischief, participants in the Capitol attack such as Jake Angeli and Ashli Babbitt) demonstrating how online conspiracy adherence has translated into offline actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic patterns of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey-based demographic patterns showing who is most likely to believe QAnon claims: higher prevalence among Republicans and Trump supporters; concentrated among white Americans and white evangelical Protestants; notable support among Hispanic Protestants and varied levels across other religious and racial groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites multiple surveys (PRRI, AEI) with percentage breakdowns by party, religion, and race, and notes increases in belief over time (e.g., 14% in 2021 rising to higher percentages in later surveys, and 32% among Trump-supporting Republicans in one 2024 poll).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media and app-based metrics as indicators of activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative indicators of QAnon activity include proportions of tweets or accounts promoting related hashtags (e.g., one in 50 tweets about voting from QAnon accounts; two in 25 #voterfraud accounts were QAnon), the popularity of apps (QDrops on app stores), and counts of discussion videos on platforms like YouTube.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics are used in the article to demonstrate the scale of dissemination and the reach of QAnon messaging online, and to document how the movement organizes and spreads content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conspiracy narratives to support political/legal campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: QAnon adherents and influencers supported and promoted legal and political efforts to overturn the 2020 election, including propagating theories about Dominion Voting Systems, promoting 'Italygate', supporting fake electors, and submitting conspiracy-backed filings and affidavits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page links QAnon activity to concrete political actions—lawsuits, fake electors plots, and coordination with political actors—showing how conspiratorial claims were operationalized in attempts to change official outcomes.
